stops.name: Tarascon, word of a son: Giovanni, renamed Frances
stops.campa: Word travels the cloth roads to Provence: in 1181, while Pietro was away in France on trade, Pica bore a son. She dreamed the boy would become a leader and baptized him Giovanni in honor of John the Baptist, and she is raising him in music, lyric song, the voice of nature, Latin and Provençal. When Pietro returned he named the boy Frances: in honor of the French culture of his mother, the romantic poetry of the troubadour, the exquisite cloth of Provence, and the family Bourlémont. Pierre hears his own gift ring in every syllable of the new name.

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont: sub rosa, the treatise of love
stops.campa: In the year the chaplain Andreas Capellanus writes his treatise De Amore, the book reaches the halls of Bourlémont, and Pierre reads of young Walter, soldier of love, whose amorous attachment is a wound he suffers. The value of secrecy is central: the most ennobling love is clandestine, and operates under the erotic principles of the rose. Pierre, who learned Bijan's cipher at Ganja, recognizes the doctrine at once. He hangs a single red rose above the hall where the songs are sung: what is spoken beneath it is spoken sub rosa, sealed, amplified by the veil.

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont, sire de Bourlémont
stops.campa: Pierre's father Simon dies, and Pierre becomes sire de Bourlémont, lord of the castle above the Meuse and of Greux and Domrémy below it. The traveler now keeps the tower he was born in; the boy who carried poems among the bales now weighs the rents of two villages and the homage of the marches. But the lordship sings. The halls of the Meuse learn the melodies of the Rhône and of the Ganjachay, and the children of Domrémy, dancing at the beech tree, dance on the land of a lord who believes their fairies have colleagues in Persia.

stops.name: Joinville, the marriage to Félicité de Joinville
stops.campa: At Joinville on the Marne, Pierre weds Félicité de Joinville: the first tie between his house and the great family of the seneschals of Champagne. The match is trade and diplomacy of the oldest kind, but Pierre courts her as a troubadour, all the same: the profession of love aloud, since shyness is a sin; the songs at the wall. To the halls of Bourlémont comes a lady of the Marne with a dowry of alliances, and the two rivers of his boyhood, Meuse and Rhône, are joined by a third.

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont, word from Assisi: the renunciation
stops.campa: Word comes north on the cloth roads: Pica's son has renounced his inheritance before the bishop of Assisi, stripped himself of his clothes, his father's wealth and the very name Bernardone, and stood naked bearing his broken heart in full humility. And Pica consoled him: we have the same name; I am Giovanna and you are Giovanni; we are John, Joan, Jeanne and Juana; we share the fire of poets, bards and troubadours; you are always my son and a Bourlémont. Pierre, reading, knows the fire she means. He lit it, singing, in a hall in Provence.

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont, the birth of Joffrey
stops.campa: Félicité bears Pierre his only son, and they name him Joffrey. He is born into a tide of spiritual energy centered on the power of youth that is rising across France; within a year the boy-shepherd Stephen of Cloyes will raise his Children's Crusade, and Joffrey will grow up on the stories, dreaming of leading pilgrims under the banner of the rose cross. Pierre holds the infant on the ramparts and shows him the valley: Domrémy, the beech, the roads. A father and a son who travel together, Nizami said, are spared nothing except not knowing one another.

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont: the Pope kisses the friar's feet
stops.campa: More word from Italy, told at the hearth with the baby Joffrey listening before he can understand: Pica's son, through his dedication to poverty and service, has gathered a brotherhood, and his weakness grew so powerful that Pope Innocent III called him to Rome, bowed, kissed his bare feet, and signed an official order for his order. Pierre laughs until he weeps. The fifth suffering, to love God and be loved back even more, has found its practitioner, and the practice of the fourth, alms, has been turned inside out: the beggar is the richest man in Italy.

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont: setting out with Joffrey, twelve years old
stops.campa: When Joffrey turns twelve, Pierre takes his only son to Italy. He hopes the experience will be as formative as his own journey with his father to the Caucasus was; the symmetry is deliberate, a rite of the house. Both of them are curious to meet the dirty friar, and Pierre feels it is important that Joffrey know his older cousin and profit from the connection in his eventual crusade. The baggage is light: cloth for gifts, the old Persian scrolls, a boy's new cipher-tablet. Father and son ride south from the Meuse as the leaves turn.

stops.name: Tarascon, the halls where he sang for Pica
stops.campa: The road to Italy bends through Provence, and Pierre shows his son the finca of the cloth branch: the corridors he filled with singing forty years ago, the hall where a red rose hung, the river the magpie flew across. He tells Joffrey the five sufferings as they walk the empty salons: profession, pilgrimage, fast, alms, prayer, the way Nizami told him the dragons, slowly, watching the boy. The second suffering is the traveler's own: longing across the extension of space and time. That is why we pilgrimage, he says, and they ride on east.

stops.name: Greccio, arrival on Christmas Eve
stops.campa: Father and son arrive at Greccio on Christmas Eve, the mountain hamlet above the Rieti valley where the friar cousin keeps this Nativity. The village is full of torches climbing the dark hillside; the friars sing; the whole valley seems to be walking toward one cave. Pierre and Joffrey take lodging among the pilgrims. Somewhere above them in the rock is the man whose naming Pierre heard ring with his own gift: Giovanni who became Frances for the honor of the cloth, the troubadour poetry and the family Bourlémont. Tomorrow they will greet him as kin.

stops.name: Greccio, communion from the friar cousin
stops.campa: In the morning Pierre and Joffrey receive communion from the hands of the friar Bourlémont himself: Pica's son, their own blood. The wafer passes from the scarred hands of the poor man of Assisi to the lord of the fairy tree and his boy. No cloth, no silver, no letters of credit: this is the family trade transacted at last in its true currency. Pierre watches his son take the host from the friar's fingers and feels the generations close like a clasp: the gift he sang into Pica in Provence returned to his own child as sacrament.

stops.name: Greccio, the cave of the first nativity
stops.campa: That night they visit the cave where the cousin has made a beautiful recreation of the Christmas manger: many lanterns lighting the scene, an ox and an ass, men costumed as magi from far lands, a Virgin and a Joseph, and among the piles of golden hay the child of Bethlehem. Joffrey is struck by the poverty of his Lord's birthplace, seen with his own eyes. Pierre is pleased that the magi resemble those he saw with Nizami: the stories he told Pica now embodied as art and faith. He holds his son's hand while waves of heat emanate from his frail cousin at prayer before the scene.
